clues: I express financial loss as a percentage relative to the original cost price!
To calculate me, you divide total loss by cost price and multiply by 100.
Buying at $20 and selling at $16 loses $4, which equals a 20% loss.
Merchants minimize my percentage during clearance markdowns.
I am Loss Percentage: relative percentage loss calculated on cost price.

educationalInfo.definition: Loss percentage measures the relative financial loss against original cost price.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Dividing loss by selling price instead of cost price.
educationalInfo.funFact: Loss percentage helps retailers evaluate clearance item write-offs!

speed.name: Speed
speed.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I measure how fast an object covers distance over time!
My formula is distance traveled divided by time taken.
A car traveling 60 miles in 1 hour has a value of 60 mph.
Speedometers display my current magnitude in vehicles.
I am Speed: scalar measure of distance covered per unit time.

educationalInfo.definition: Speed is the rate at which an object covers distance over time.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing speed (scalar) with velocity (vector with direction).
educationalInfo.funFact: Light travels at the universal maximum speed of 300,000 km per second!

distance.name: Distance
distance.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I measure the total length of path traveled between two physical locations!
My formula is speed multiplied by time traveled.
Traveling at 50 mph for 2 hours covers a total length of 100 miles.
Odometer dials track my cumulative total in automobiles.
I am Distance: total length of path covered by a moving object.

educationalInfo.definition: Distance is the total length of space between two points along a path.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing total distance with shortest displacement vector.
educationalInfo.funFact: Distance is always non-negative in classical geometry!

time_taken.name: Time Taken
time_taken.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I measure the duration required to complete a trip or physical motion!
My formula is total distance divided by speed.
Covering 120 miles at 60 mph requires a duration of 2 hours.
Stopwatches and clocks record my elapsed measurement.
I am Time Taken: duration required to traverse a given distance.

educationalInfo.definition: Time taken is the duration required to cover a specified distance at a given speed.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to match time units between speed and distance.
educationalInfo.funFact: Time dilation occurs near light speed in Einstein relativity!

work_rate.name: Work Rate
work_rate.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I measure the fraction of a total job completed by a worker in one unit of time!
If a painter finishes a job in 5 hours, my rate per hour is 1/5.
Faster workers have larger values for my rate per hour.
Combining individual values determines joint completion speed.
I am Work Rate: fraction of total work completed per unit time.
hints: Fraction of job done per unit time.

educationalInfo.definition: Work rate is the portion of a total task completed in one time unit.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Adding total completion times directly instead of adding work rates.
educationalInfo.funFact: Work rate problems assume uniform efficiency throughout a job!

time_required.name: Time Required
time_required.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I measure the total time needed for a worker or team to finish a complete project!
I am calculated as the reciprocal of the combined work rate.
If joint work rate is 1/3 per hour, total duration required is 3 hours.
Project managers estimate project schedules using my value.
I am Time Required: total elapsed time needed to complete a task.
hints: Total hours or days to complete task.

educationalInfo.definition: Time required is the total duration taken to finish an entire task.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Assuming double the workers takes double the time.
educationalInfo.funFact: Adding more workers reduces time required in inverse proportion!

individual_efficiency.name: Individual Efficiency
individual_efficiency.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I measure the relative speed and work output capability of a single worker!
A worker who completes a task in 2 hours is twice as efficient as one taking 4 hours.
I determine how individual contributions combine in team projects.
Employers evaluate job performance using my productivity measure.
I am Individual Efficiency: individual work capability per unit time.

educationalInfo.definition: Individual efficiency reflects the speed and productivity of a single worker.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Assuming all workers possess identical individual efficiency.
educationalInfo.funFact: Efficiency ratios allow scaling team output estimates accurately!

combined_work_rate.name: Combined Work Rate
combined_work_rate.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the total joint work rate achieved when multiple workers collaborate together!
To calculate me, you add individual work rates together: 1/A + 1/B.
If worker A does 1/4 per hour and B does 1/4 per hour, our combined rate is 1/2 per hour.
Collaborative teams finish projects faster due to my combined rate.
I am Combined Work Rate: sum of individual work rates working together.

educationalInfo.definition: Combined work rate is the total portion of work completed per unit time by collaborating workers.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Adding individual completion times instead of rates.
educationalInfo.funFact: Teamwork increases combined work rate and reduces total completion time!

gross_amount.name: Gross Amount
gross_amount.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the total price or invoice value before any tax deductions or discounts!
Deducting taxes or discounts from me yields the final net amount.
An invoice billing $100 before tax sets my value to $100.
Accountants use my total as the starting baseline for tax calculations.
I am Gross Amount: total bill amount prior to taxes or deductions.
hints: Total price before taxes or deductions.

educationalInfo.definition: Gross amount is the full total price before any deductions, discounts, or taxes.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing gross amount with net amount after taxes.
educationalInfo.funFact: Gross income refers to earnings before payroll taxes are withheld!

net_price.name: Net Price
net_price.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the final net price paid after adding taxes or applying discounts to the gross amount!
Adding 10% tax to a $100 gross bill makes my final price $110.
I represent the actual out of pocket cost on customer store receipts.
Shoppers pay my final calculated value at check out registers.
I am Net Price: final price after accounting for taxes and discounts.
hints: Final price including taxes or discounts.

educationalInfo.definition: Net price is the actual final price paid after all additions and deductions.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing net price with original wholesale cost.
educationalInfo.funFact: Net price reflects true consumer expenditure after tax!

tax_deducted.name: Tax Deducted
tax_deducted.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the exact monetary amount of tax subtracted or added in a financial transaction!
To calculate me, you multiply gross amount by the applicable tax percentage rate.
On a $100 item with 10% tax, my value equals $10.
Tax receipts display my specific dollar contribution clearly.
I am Tax Deducted: monetary value of tax calculated on a gross sum.

educationalInfo.definition: Tax deducted is the specific monetary sum withheld or levied as tax.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing tax rate percentage with tax monetary amount.
educationalInfo.funFact: Tax deducted at source (TDS) is a common income tax collection method!

face_value.name: Face Value
face_value.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the original nominal value of a stock share printed on a company certificate!
Dividends are calculated as a percentage of my fixed printed value.
A share issued with $10 printed value retains $10 as my permanent nominal worth.
Unlike market price, my nominal printed value does not fluctuate daily.
I am Face Value: fixed nominal value printed on a stock or bond certificate.

educationalInfo.definition: Face value is the nominal value of a security stated by its issuer.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing face value with fluctuating market trading price.
educationalInfo.funFact: Dividends are always declared as a percentage of face value!

market_value.name: Market Value
market_value.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the current trading price at which a stock share buys or sells in the stock exchange!
My value fluctuates daily based on market supply and demand.
A share with $10 face value might trade on the stock exchange at my price of $25.
Investors calculate total portfolio worth using my current price.
I am Market Value: current market trading price of a share.
hints: Used to buy or sell shares.

educationalInfo.definition: Market value is the current price at which an asset or security can be bought or sold.
examples: Share trading at $25 on stock market
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Calculating dividend amounts using market value instead of face value.
educationalInfo.funFact: Market value reflects investor expectations of company performance!

market_value.hint: Used to buy or sell shares.

annual_yield.name: Annual Yield
annual_yield.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I measure the real percentage return earned on an investment relative to its market cost!
To calculate me, you divide annual dividend earned by market investment cost and multiply by 100.
Earning $10 annual dividend on a share bought at $100 market price gives 10% yield.
Investors compare stock returns using my yield percentage.
I am Annual Yield: percentage return on market value invested.

educationalInfo.definition: Annual yield measures the percentage return an investor receives relative to current market price.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Calculating yield based on face value instead of market price.
educationalInfo.funFact: Higher annual yield indicates greater cash return per dollar invested!
